```{r setup, include = FALSE}
# HTML figures are drawn as PNG and kept as WebP: lossless (the same pixels in about half the space of PNG), or
# lossy at quality 90 when that is less than half the size, as for traces and densities of thousands of draws. The
# PDF figures stay vector graphics. Any failure of magick (not installed, no WebP, or a broken installation whose
# system libraries are missing) keeps the PNG
webp <- function(path) {
  if (knitr::is_latex_output() || !grepl(pattern = "[.]png$", x = path)) return(path)
  tryCatch(
      {
        if (!requireNamespace("magick", quietly = TRUE) || !isTRUE(magick::magick_config()$webp)) return(path)
        img <- magick::image_read(path)
        out <- sub(pattern = "[.]png$", replacement = ".webp", x = path)
        tmp <- tempfile(fileext = ".webp")
        magick::image_write(
            image   = img
          , path    = out
          , format  = "webp"
          , quality = 100
          , defines = c(`webp:lossless` = "true")
          )
        magick::image_write(image = img, path = tmp, format = "webp", quality = 90)
        if (file.size(tmp) < file.size(out) / 2) file.copy(from = tmp, to = out, overwrite = TRUE)
        unlink(c(path, tmp))
        out
      }
    , error = function(e) path
    )
}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = FALSE, comment = "", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 5,
                      dev = if (knitr::is_latex_output()) "cairo_pdf" else "ragg_png", dpi = 96,
                      fig.process = webp)
if (requireNamespace("baystability", quietly = TRUE)) library(baystability) else
  pkgload::load_all(export_all = FALSE, helpers = FALSE, quiet = TRUE)
```

# Abstract

The sites regression (SREG) model puts the genotype main effects into the bilinear terms, so its biplot shows which
genotypes do best where. This vignette fits it with the first year as prior, then shows how the weight of the earlier
trial changes the posterior and how WAIC chooses the number of terms.

# The SREG model with the first year as prior

```{r sreg}
fs <-
  bayes_ammi(
      .data       = cultivo2009
    , .y          = y
    , .gen        = entry
    , .env        = site
    , .rep        = rep
    , .nIter      = 3000
    , .prior_data = cultivo2008
    , .n0         = NULL
    , .model      = "SREG"
    , .k          = 2
    , .burnin     = 1000
    , .thin       = 1
    , .chains     = 2
    , .priors     = bys_priors(
          mu_mean     = 0
        , mu_var      = 1e+8
        , tau_mean    = 0
        , tau_var     = 1e+8
        , delta_mean  = 0
        , delta_var   = 1e+8
        , lambda_mean = 0
        , lambda_var  = 1e+8
        , nu          = 1
        , s2          = NULL
        )
    , .level      = 0.95
    , .seed       = 2012
    , .align      = TRUE
    , .waic       = TRUE
    )
fs
```

```{r sreg-bip, fig.width = 9}
bs <-
  bayes_gge_biplot(
      fit           = fs
    , burnin        = 0
    , thin          = 1
    , pb            = 0.05
    , plot_stable   = FALSE
    , plot_unstable = TRUE
    , ncolors       = 5
    , .which        = "both"
    , .grid         = 100
    )
bs$biplot
```

On an SREG biplot the first axis reflects mostly the genotype means, so genotypes far out on it are above or below
average rather than interacting.

# The weight of the earlier trial

`.n0` sets how many observations per cell the earlier trial counts for. By default it is its number of replicates
(3).

```{r n0}
w <- c(0.5, 3, 12)
res <-
  data.table::rbindlist(
      l = lapply(
          X   = w
        , FUN = function(n0) {
            f <-
              bayes_ammi(
                  .data       = cultivo2009
                , .y          = y
                , .gen        = entry
                , .env        = site
                , .rep        = rep
                , .nIter      = 1500
                , .prior_data = cultivo2008
                , .n0         = n0
                , .model      = "AMMI"
                , .k          = 2
                , .burnin     = 500
                , .thin       = 1
                , .chains     = 1
                , .priors     = bys_priors(
                      mu_mean     = 0
                    , mu_var      = 1e+8
                    , tau_mean    = 0
                    , tau_var     = 1e+8
                    , delta_mean  = 0
                    , delta_var   = 1e+8
                    , lambda_mean = 0
                    , lambda_var  = 1e+8
                    , nu          = 1
                    , s2          = NULL
                    )
                , .level      = 0.95
                , .seed       = 4
                , .align      = TRUE
                , .waic       = TRUE
                )
            data.table::data.table(
                n0      = n0
              , mu      = f$summary[parameter == "mu", mean]
              , alpha1  = f$summary[block == "tau", mean][1]
              , lambda1 = f$summary[parameter == "lambda[1]", mean]
              )
          }
        )
    )
res
```

```{r n0f, include = FALSE}
m08 <-
  bys_ls_means(
      .data = cultivo2008
    , .y    = y
    , .gen  = entry
    , .env  = site
    )$grand_mean
m09 <-
  bys_ls_means(
      .data = cultivo2009
    , .y    = y
    , .gen  = entry
    , .env  = site
    )$grand_mean
```

As $n_0$ grows the posterior moves from the second year (grand mean `r round(m09)`) towards the first
(`r round(m08)`). With $n_0 = 3$ it sits halfway. A small $n_0$ is the choice when the earlier trial was grown under
different conditions.

# How many terms?

WAIC compares fits with different numbers of terms (Watanabe 2010; Vehtari et al. 2017):

```{r terms}
fits <-
  lapply(
      X   = c(1, 2, 3, 5)
    , FUN = function(K) {
        bayes_ammi(
            .data       = cultivo2009
          , .y          = y
          , .gen        = entry
          , .env        = site
          , .rep        = rep
          , .nIter      = 1500
          , .prior_data = cultivo2008
          , .n0         = NULL
          , .model      = "AMMI"
          , .k          = K
          , .burnin     = 500
          , .thin       = 1
          , .chains     = 1
          , .priors     = bys_priors(
                mu_mean     = 0
              , mu_var      = 1e+8
              , tau_mean    = 0
              , tau_var     = 1e+8
              , delta_mean  = 0
              , delta_var   = 1e+8
              , lambda_mean = 0
              , lambda_var  = 1e+8
              , nu          = 1
              , s2          = NULL
              )
          , .level      = 0.95
          , .seed       = 5
          , .align      = TRUE
          , .waic       = TRUE
          )
      }
    )
names(fits) <- paste0("K", c(1, 2, 3, 5))
cp <- do.call(what = bys_compare, args = fits)
cp
```

```{r termsf, include = FALSE}
t <- cp$table
close <- t$model[t$dWAIC <= 2 * t$dWAIC_se]
```

WAIC prefers `r t$model[1]`; `r paste(setdiff(close, t$model[1]), collapse = " and ")` lie within two standard errors
of the difference (`dWAIC_se`), so the data do not separate them. With the first year as a strong prior, the
singular values of every term are pulled towards that year's, and few terms suffice for prediction. The paper chose
three terms with the Bayes factor, which compares the marginal likelihoods of the models rather than their
predictive accuracy.

Perez-Elizalde, S., Jarquin, D. and Crossa, J. (2012). A general Bayesian estimation method of linear-bilinear models applied to plant breeding trials with genotype x environment interaction. *Journal of Agricultural, Biological, and Environmental Statistics*, 17, 15--37. doi:10.1007/s13253-011-0063-9

Yan, W., Hunt, L. A., Sheng, Q. and Szlavnics, Z. (2000). Cultivar evaluation and mega-environment investigation based on the GGE biplot. *Crop Science*, 40(3), 597--605.

Watanabe, S. (2010). Asymptotic equivalence of Bayes cross validation and widely applicable information criterion in singular learning theory. *Journal of Machine Learning Research*, 11, 3571--3594.

Vehtari, A., Gelman, A. and Gabry, J. (2017). Practical Bayesian model evaluation using leave-one-out cross-validation and WAIC. *Statistics and Computing*, 27(5), 1413--1432.
